analysis.one_liner: Replaces federal income, estate, and gift taxes with a single flat tax on wages and business profits.
analysis.headline: The flat tax bill drew 7 cosponsors, never got a committee vote, and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Dick Armey's flat tax would replace the entire federal income tax with a single 19% rate, dropping to 17%, applied to wages and business profits. It would repeal the estate and gift taxes, the alternative minimum tax, every tax credit, and nearly every deduction, and it would let employers reclaim surplus assets from their pension plans. Only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits would be taxed — income from investments would be tax-free.
analysis.who_benefits: Households living mainly on investment income would owe no individual income tax at all, because the bill taxes only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment benefits — leaving interest, dividends, capital gains, and rents untaxed. Heirs to large estates would keep the entire inheritance, since the estate and gift taxes would be repealed retroactively to December 31, 2000. Employers with overfunded pension plans could pull the surplus out of the plan without paying the excise tax that previously applied, and pension plans would no longer have to follow nondiscrimination rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, large estates, and employers

how_it_helps.text: Households whose income comes from investments rather than a paycheck would pay zero individual income tax, because taxable income is defined as only wages, retirement distributions, and unemployment compensation above a standard deduction.
The estate and gift taxes would be repealed outright, and the repeal would apply retroactively to estates of people who died after December 31, 2000, erasing tax liability that already existed.

Employers could reclaim excess assets from overfunded pension plans and pay them to themselves as ordinary income, because the bill repeals the excise tax on such reversions and loosens the rules on transferring the money out.

Pension plans would no longer have to cover lower-paid workers fairly: the bill repeals nondiscrimination, minimum-coverage, top-heavy, and contribution-limit rules that stop plans from being designed mostly for executives.
The alternative minimum tax, which forces high-income households to pay at least some tax despite deductions, would be repealed entirely.

Title II would amend House and Senate rules to require a three-fifths vote to raise income tax rates, cut the standard deduction, or add any tax break that reduces revenue — locking the new low rates in against future Congresses.

analysis.who_pays: Working households would still pay Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, but would lose every tax credit — including the Earned Income Tax Credit that supplements low wages — and deductions such as mortgage interest, charitable giving, and state and local taxes, since taxable income would count only wages, pensions, and unemployment benefits. Workers at companies with overfunded pensions could see the surplus pulled out by the employer. The federal government would collect far less revenue, meaning either deeper debt or cuts to spending on services. Public and nonprofit employees would face a new 19% tax on the value of noncash benefits like health insurance, paid by their employer.
analysis.who_pays_short: Wage earners and workers with pensions

drawbacks.text: Every tax credit would be repealed, including the Earned Income Tax Credit, which puts money back in the paychecks of low-wage working families; combined with the loss of refundable credits, taxes on many low-income workers would go up even under a lower headline rate.

Homeowners would lose the mortgage interest deduction and charitable givers the charitable deduction, because taxable income would be defined only as wages, pensions, and unemployment benefits above a standard deduction.

Repealing the tax on pension surplus reversions and the pension nondiscrimination rules would make it easier for companies to pull money out of worker retirement plans and to design plans that favor executives over rank-and-file employees.

The three-fifths supermajority requirement in Title II would make it far harder for any future Congress to raise rates or close loopholes, entrenching the new tax structure even if it proved unworkable or unfair.

With investment income and inheritances untaxed while wages are taxed at 19%, the burden of funding the federal government would shift toward people who work for a living, and the large revenue loss would have to be made up through debt or spending cuts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's real selling point — simplicity — is genuine: most households would compute tax by subtracting a large standard deduction from their paycheck and applying one rate. The large standard deduction would also take many low-income families off the tax rolls entirely. But the design pays for that simplicity by exempting investment income and inheritances while keeping payroll taxes on wages, and by stripping out the Earned Income Tax Credit and every other credit. The pension provisions go further, letting employers raid surpluses and drop fairness rules. On balance, the benefits flow overwhelmingly to households at the top and to employers, while the costs fall on wage earners and on the Treasury.

outcome.mechanism: The bill went to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: House Majority Leader Dick Armey introduced the flat tax bill on March 15, 2001, joined by five colleagues including Reps. Myrick, Toomey, Hefley, Smith of Michigan, and Sununu.
The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, for parts of it, to the Rules Committee.
Seven members cosponsored the bill — six Republicans and one Democrat.
No further action was ever recorded: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wage earners and low-income working families are better off that the bill never advanced, since they would have lost the Earned Income Tax Credit and every other credit and deduction. The bill's intended beneficiaries — high earners, large estates, and employers with overfunded pensions — gained nothing because it never became law.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so the only measure of support is sponsorship: 7 cosponsors, 6 of them Republicans and 1 a Democrat, all in a chamber with 223 Republicans and 208 Democrats.

industries.note: Investment income — interest, dividends, capital gains, rents — would go completely untaxed, and the estate and gift taxes would be repealed retroactively. The bill taxes only paychecks, so its largest gains flow to people who live on wealth rather than wages, funded by a bigger burden on workers and the Treasury.

The bill repeals the excise tax on companies pulling surplus assets out of their pension plans and eases the transfer rules, letting employers reclaim the money. Workers in those plans lose the protection that kept surplus funds in their retirement system.

The bill repeals nondiscrimination, coverage, contribution-limit, and early-withdrawal-penalty rules, freeing plans from compliance costs and restrictions. The same repeal removes the rules that keep workplace retirement plans fair to lower-paid employees.

A new 19% tax would apply to the value of noncash benefits — such as employer-provided health insurance — that tax-exempt organizations and federal, state, and local governments provide their employees. That raises the cost of public and nonprofit employment.

With taxable income defined only as wages, pensions, and unemployment benefits, the mortgage interest deduction would disappear, weakening the tax incentive that supports home purchases and mortgage lending.
